There is a policy and a principle involved in the second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think it advisable for the House to pass such legislation in view of the fact that a royal commission has been appointed to make recommendations in regard to the very matters contained in this bill. We were told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when leader of the opposition last June, at page 5133 of Hansard, that such a commission should be appointed in view of the very large revenue handled by this department, and he said that the commission should be composed of three judges, one nominated by the government, one by the op-

We conferred among ourselves as to the manner in which that all important end could best be attained, and we came to the conclusion that the manner in which that end could best be attained would be through the appointment of a commission of judges, three in number, one to be named by the prime minister of the day, the second to be named by the leader of the opposition, and the third to be named by the leader of the Progressive party. I submit, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to say it as emphatically as I can, that I believe it is a commission c>f that character, and of that character alone, that the people of this eounti'y will be satisfied with on this all-important national problem.
That commission was never appointed, but another commission was substituted for it and they are simply continuing the work of the old committee of this House which brought out the facts in this connection. In view of this I think it due the House and the country that the Prime Minister or the Minister of Customs and Excise should explain why this roving commission is going about the country from one city to the other, finding out nothing which has not already been discovered by the committee of this House which investigated this department. For that reason I think this bill should stand until such time as we have the report of this commission, if it is ever received. There has been a rightabout-face made by the government, and in view of that we should have some expression of opinion from the government as to when that report may be expected and as to whether it will contain anything along the line of this bill. Why is this commission spending hundreds of thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money if they are not going to recommend the co-ordination of all these different departments in order that they may be administered with greater efficiency, as the public utilities of this country are not at present administered, ;n my opinion? For that reason I am opposed to the second reading of this bill; I think it should stand over until we have received the report of this commission.

I would go further and say that that decision should be the only decision called for, except that an appeal might be made to the minister after such finding was made. Then the minister would find himself in this position- which I think would be a much more happy one than under the former procedure-that if an appeal were made to him by business men, or by political friends, or by anyone at all, he would be able to present to those people the final decision of the department in regard to the case-a given seizure we will say-and then, whether he changed that decision or overrode it, he would have to superimpose his finding upon that of the department and would have to take the final responsibility. It is easy to see what would happen. I think the duties which they perform are of such great importance that they ought to be fixed by statute; we ought to fix in this statute the responsibilities which these officers shall bear, and among them is the one I have mentioned. For instance, in connection with customs, a definite determination in the matter of the disposal of a seizure should be made by the department, and that should be conclusive except that an appeal might rest to the minister; I have no objection to that, but let there be a decision bj' the departmental officials before such an appeal is possible. The same thing applies to sales tax, and the same thing would apply, in a measure, I presume, to income tax and excise tax. The principle I am advocating is that the departmental officials should make a decision in all these cases, and if a change in their decision is made, it must be one that shall appear on these documents themselves, as being superimposed upon the department by the ministerial head.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: I quite realize that, but what prevents the official, before he gives his written decision, from consulting with the minister? Nothing whatever.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
But if he is called in
question he cannot hide behind the minister. He must stand by his written decision because the law would lay that responsibility upon him.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: But his written decision may have been affected by his consultation with the minister. I have had some experience in the matter.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
He cannot take refuge
in the statement that he consulted his minister and the minister so instructed him. If I had my way the minister would have no right to instruct his officers. That is the point I am making. As the matter stands now I could gq down to the Customs department and blindly pick out literally hundreds of decisions as regards which, if you cornered the official and asked him why he made the decision, he would tell you he made it after consultation with the minister.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: How can you carry on otherwise? If you prevent an official of the department from consulting with his minister, I do not see how the work can be carried on. I do not see how you could possibly have it otherwise.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
I am not trying to prevent that, but I would fix the responsibility. I would say further that when I went into

Department oj National Revenue
that office there were some 2,200 of these documents piled on tables waiting for the decision of the minister. I became ill trying to caitch up with them and my hon. friend took up the task while I was in the hospital.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: Could you not account for that by the fact that the inquiry was proceeding at that time?

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
No, my hon. friend is
wrong. These were ordinary routine seizures, involving trivial amounts such as $2, $5, a pair of silk stockings and I remember one seizure of a bonnet which was smuggled in. My point is that form K-9 should be changed so that all such matters would be disposed of by the signature of the commissioner, and the minister would never see them unless the decision of the commissioner was appealed.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: I am not criticising the suggestion of my hon. friend, but that does not need to be fixed by statute. Surely you have sufficient confidence in a minister of the crown to allow him to give the necessary instructions, either through orders in council or by departmental rules.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
I have confidence in this minister, of course, and I think so long as he is there that will be done. I am equally persuaded of this fact, though, that as we drift away from this controversy which arose last year, affairs in the department may revert to their previous condition. Let me read what the final report of the special committee contained :
The evidence submitted to the committee leads to the general conclusion that for a long time the Department of Customs and Excise had been slowly degenerating in efficiency....
I want to try, by statutory arrangement, to minimize that tendency to slow degeneration, and I want to say very frankly that I have every confidence in the present minister. But he knows very well, as we all know, that like others he will leave that office and others will step in. They may come from this side of the House or the other side; I do not care what their politics may be; familiarity breeds contempt, and I Want to surround that department from the experience of the past with such safeguards as will very largely eliminate that tendency. Let me state further that a high official of the government such as the commissioner of customs, and his immediate assistants, in handling these matters of routine day after day is more likely
to be precise and exact than is the minister who is open to appeal from his friends all over the country, and to whom people believe they have a right to appeal. I am not even going to prevent that, but if I have my way the decision of the executive officers of the department, of the professional staff if you like, shall be definitely given before the minister has an opportunity to change it. That is my point.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: Referring to subsection 4 of section 2 I would ask how this bill affects the status of the present employees of this department, because I do not see anything at all in the bill which maintains their standing. I suppose it is the intention of the government that those who are now employed shall continue to be employed by the new department, and that it will not be necessary to reappoint those officials who are in office at present. There is another matter, in connection with the salaries of the employees of this and other departments. If we can believe reports which appeared in the Ottawa papers, the Prime Minister stated the night before the election that there would be a salary revision and that it would be brought up at this session, but so far we have seen no evidence of it, and it is now suggested that it will be left over until a later time, I think that would be most unfair; the matter has been too long delayed already. In supporting the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) I would suggest to the minister that while it is necessary in the reorganization of the department to cut out all the dead wood, at the same time those men who remain in the service should receive a fair and adequate salary. I believe they should receive reasonable salaries in any event, which is not the case with some of them at the present.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
The question now raised
by my hon. friend has no direct connection with this bill, since it concerns the civil service at large. The salary revision is now under consideration and will be dealt with in due course.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend that the passing of this act has no effect whatever on the officials now employed by the department; they remain in just the same position.

Department of National Revenue

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: I would like to back up the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). After last session I cannot help but feel that a great many of the decisions made in the department for some years before the investigation would never have been made at all if the deputy minister had been responsible for them, and if the minister had to accept sole responsibility for any reversal of that decision. A great deal of the trouble seemed to arise because of the fact that' responsibility was not fixed in that way. I do not see any reason why a minister should have to deal with the routine business of the department; I do not believe he has the time and I do not believe he is half so well qualified to do so as the deputy minister, I believe the minister would save himself a good deal of trouble if he would adopt that suggestion. It was perfectly obvious from the evidence last year that the minister was constantly bothered with people who were supposed to have influence with him in dealing with cases connected with smuggling. It appeared to be a regular thing for people who were influential in the party to which the minister belonged to plead with him in connection with these cases. I do not know why that consideration should obtain at all in a case concerning smuggling or a breach of the law. It was simply an effort to use political influence in order to have the fine or penalty made smaller, and for that reason I believe the routine business and the decisions so far as possible should be attended to by the deputy minister, who should take the responsibility. Then if the minister wishes to reverse that decision he may do so, and in so doing clear the deputy minister of all responsibility.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
I do not want to prolong the discussion, but I would not like the impression to go abroad-which might happen from the remarks of my hon. friend-that it is not the intention of the department in future to have the decisions made by the commissioner of customs, we will say. It is the intention of the department that the minister shall [Mr Euler.]
make these decisions-in fact that these cases shall never come to the minister for decision at all.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: You said it was intended that the minister should make the decision.

speechtext:
I think I can see a very
happy way out of this little difficulty, and I should not like to pass this clause with any feeling that either myself or any other members of the committee were not fully satisfied. Would the minister consider amending the Customs Act-I think the same thing would apply to the Excise Act-particularly such sections as 174, 175, 176 and 177 which deal with this very question? I have not the act itself under my hand, but there is a resume of it in paragraph 7 of the report of the committee of investigation of last year. I will read this briefly and then the committee will see exactly what my point is.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
What are the sections of

speechtext:
I am going to quote
paragraph 7 of the report of the special parliamentary committee, if the minister has it.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: But referring to what sections of the Customs Act?

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext:
Sections 174, 175, 176 and 177. The paragraph which I desire to quote reads as follows:
Upon making a seizure the collector or seizing officer forthwith reports the circumstances of the case to the commissioner of customs (section 174). Thereupon the commissioner notifies the owner or claimant of the thing seized, stating tire reasons for the seizure, and calls upon such owner or claimant to furnish within thirty days any evidence he may desire to submit, (section 175). After the expiration of thirty days or sooner, if evidence is forthcoming on the part of the owner or claimant, "the commissioner may consider and weigh the circumstances of the case and report his opinion and recommendation thereon to the minister".
I pause here to suggest that instead of saying that it should be amended to say "he shall thereupon make his decision." That is, instead of the commissioner reporting his opinion and recommendations, he shall make a decision on this evidence. That is section 176. I continue reading:
The minister thereupon either gives, his decision and states the terms upon which the thing seized or detained may be released or the penalty or forfeiture remitted or refers the decision to the court (section 177).
Now my point is this. The minister should amend the act so as to impose the responsibility for the decision upon the commissioner,
and then add a clause to provide that the claimant may make an appeal to the minister or to the governor in council-to whatever body he may choose. But if the committee can get my idea of this matter, and if the minister himself would appreciate it, I think it will save untold trouble in the future. That is let the officers of the department decide under the law and by the law what the disposition of the case shall foe. Let there be an appeal to the government through the minister, or to the minister himself if he will, but let the officer make the decision. If the minister would agree to bring in an amendment to the act to give effect to these suggestions I think that would meet the case entirely.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE
speechtext: Am I correct in assuming that the suggestion is that instead of making the proposed change in the bill under discussion it should be made in the Customs Act?

speechtext: Yes. I believe the minister is sympathetic towards my viewpoint and that he wants to accomplish the same end as I do.

subtopic: REORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENT OF CUSTOMS AND EXCISE

The machinery is now being provided for correcting that, and I believe that under the minister it will be put into force. I want to express my pleasure that this is being done because I believe it will result in greater efficiency in collecting the revenues.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved that the House go into chmmittee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting certain debts due the crown, to provide that the governor in council shall have power to make regulations providing for the apportionment and adjustment of indebtedness incurred for advances of seed grain, fodder for animals and other relief, and to discharge and release in whole or in part any moneys due to His Majesty in respect of either principal or interest or both, as may be considered equitable in the circumstances.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OR DISCHARGE OF AMOUNTS DUE ON SEED CRAIN AND OTHER ADVANCES
speechtext: This resolution undoubtedly deputes fairly wide power to the governor in council, but the negotiations will be carried on with the provincial governments, the municipalities and the loan companies. It has to do with advances that were made for seed grain and relief over a long term of years. Of course where the security has been taken and registered the crown usually gets all the money that accrues from the sale of any of the properties. In many cases the matter of adjusting these old accounts is difficult because of foreclosure proceedings having been taken by loan companies. In the southern portion of Alberta and Saskatchewan we made a new experiment. We set aside a portion of the land in those provinces that was homesteaded1, and upon which in many cases the patent was earned, and to the settlers on these lands a considerable sum of money was advanced for seed grain, for fodder and for other relief. But we are undertaking now, under a commission representative of the federal and provincial gevernments to induce the settlers on that area to discontinue agricultural pursuits and to go back to the old and tried business of ranching. This transformation has caused a good deal of trouble. I suppose seventy-five per cent of the settlers have abandoned the land, and it becomes a question of arranging an amicable adjustment of the indebtedness. There is indebtedness to machine companies, to banks, to mortgage loan companies, and indebtedness in taxation to the provincial government. The bill is intended to give the department power to deal with just such cases as that, to forego, should it be considered advisable, our right to the full indebtedness. In many cases the federal government does not get the full indebtedness and the whole thing is tied up.

subtopic: ADJUSTMENT OR DISCHARGE OF AMOUNTS DUE ON SEED CRAIN AND OTHER ADVANCES
speechtext: At present has the government a prior charge?

Seed, Grain and Other Relief

against the lands in question. I would have preferred to have the act do what we wiil have to do largely by regulation, but on account of the difficulty of that we are asking for fairly wide powers. As we are not dealing with individuals but with municipalities and provinces, it is necessary to have this power without handicap in order that the indebtedness registered against these lands may be adjusted.

It is proposed to
define the term "Dominion analyst." We have many officers in the department who under the civil service regulations are classified as chemists, or in some other way. Under this amendment it will be within the power of the lieutenant-governor in council to designate who shall be an analyst, including the chief dominion analyst and the assistant chief dominion analyst.
Would this place it within the power of the government to designate a druggist or chemist anywhere in the country as an analyst for the purpose of this act?
Yes, it would give us that power.

Will the minister explain
the reason for sub-clause (2) ?

It is proposed to
extend the definition of the word "drug" to include the use of antiseptics and prophylactics, such as vaccines.
This is a technical subject and I am sure not many of us are familiar with it. What is the need or the demand for this?

The original definition read:
"Drug" includes all medicines for internal or external use for man or animal.
It is considered by the departmental officials that that definition is not wide enough in itself and we propose to amend it to read as follows:
"Drug" includes all medicine for internal or external use for man or animal; and any substance or mixture of substances intended to be used for the treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease in man or animal.
By the addition to the section of these words, antiseptics and prophylactics such as vaccines would be considered as drugs and I think it i3 essential that they should be included.
According to this definition a mustard plaster would be included.
A mustard plaster would be all right.
A better way would be to include all drugs as contained in some standard book.
That would not give the extent or width that is desired by the department. The British Pharmacopoeia would not give you what you wish. Many drugs are being used that are not included in it.
Antiseptics are as old as the hills.

Under the present definition neither antiseptics nor prophylactics such as vaccines would be considered as drugs. At least that is the opinion of departmental officials who have been administering the act.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Regulations.

This is an important clause, dealing with the standardization of certain patent drugs. In the act as it exists to-day section 4 reads:
Recognized in the latest edition of the British Pharmacopoeia; or, recognized in the latest edition of any foreign pharmacopoeia; or which is not recognized in any pharmacopoeia but is found in some generally recognized standard work on materia medica or drugs.
It is proposed by this amendment to bring in a schedule and this would provide for a standardization outside of what is known as the usual pharmacopoeia standardization. If the hon. member will refer to schedule B, he will find that the drugs mentioned there are very potent, such as strophanthus, digitalis, ergot and other vegetable preparations, pituitrin, thyroid, adrenalin and so on. It has been found in modem practice that in order to arrive at a proper standardization for these drugs certain biological tests must be mlade. It is the purpose of this clause to provide that standards will be set up through biological tests and that those who are engaged in the manufacture of these drugs shall be licensed, shall have proper laboratories,
Food and Dings Act

and shall be subject to inspection. It is further provided that each batch of the drugs made in those laboratories shall be subject to examination by the laboratories of the Department of Health. This, I think, meets with the approval of the profession, because it is essential that these drugs shall have a standard. It will also meet with the approval of those who are engaged in t'he manufacture of these drugs, and the people generally will benefit by having better drugs.

For the last fifteen or sixteen years I have been strongly in favour of strengthening the hands of the department in connection with this Food and Drugs Act. I am, however, aware that it is possible to abuse a good thing. I am not suggesting that this act does so abuse that privilege, but what gives me a little concern is this:	we
have an act at present that is exceedingly technical. I confess it is beyond my capacity to pass any reasonable judgment on the sections as we come to them. On former occasions we usually referred this act to a special committee of the House, drafting into that committee a number of medical men and others who had some technical knowledge of the subject. It occurs to me that unless some of our professional men are in their seats and have given some study to this legislation, most of us will be acting pretty much in the dark. Moreover, this legislation undoubtedly affects those who manufacture these various serums, drugs and so on, and I recall in the past some very bitter controversies over the drafting of some previous amendments to the act. Some of these amendments I supported, some of them I strongly opposed. I am not in a position to express an opinion now, but I really think it would have been better if this act had gone to a special committee where it could have been given that detailed consideration which it merits.

While I would do anything to strengthen the hands of the department, yet I think on reading over certain clauses of this bill it is quite drastic, and abuses may easily arise. I cannot understand for a minute why under the first clause the word "antiseptic''* cannot be considered as a drug. In any school or college antiseptic is a term as old as the hills. There may be some antiseptics, if that is what the minister or the department is getting at, that are not drugs. That is the reason I would have suggested the use of some definite volume such as the British Pharmacopoeia. It is kept pretty well up to date and I do not think it would leave out very much. The second clause leaves the door open for drastic action. 
It provides for the licensing of manufacturers preparing drugs and it requires that manufacturers of the drugs mentioned submit test portions of each and every batch of such drugs and so on. All that is very good in its way, but it leaves the door open to a very great deal of drastic action which may be taken by the department as regards food and so on. I am not saying that there is anything wrong with the bill, but it leaves the door open to drastic action and we should look into it a little further. I would favour the suggestion of the hon, member for Vancouver Centre.

This act was
passed in 1920 and it has been in operation since that date. This is the first occasion that it has been in the House for further amendment and these amendments have grown out of the experience of the officers of the department. I have no objection to letting the bill go to a committee of this House, but I think the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) does not quite understand the object of the bill and the amendment. The object of the act is to protect the public against adulteration and against any deception in the quantity sold, and in the section to which I have referred I pointed out that the schedule mentioned at the 'back of the bill sets forth the drugs that are to be dealt with. They are limited in number; they are very potent drugs, and while we as practitioners strive to get the best possible, the standards vary in different countries. Standards vary even in different laboratories, and in dealing with potent drugs of this character I think we should have the highest quality as a standard; that is done to-day by physiological tests. I cannot see why the medical profession would take any exception to this amendment; in fact I know that nothing will please them more than to have these particular drugs standardized. If that is to be done and if this benefit is to be secured to the public then it is essential that the establishments be checked, that they be required to take out a license and to maintain a proper laboratory, subject to inspection. We are not amending a medical act; this is a food and drug act designed to give protection to the public. So I would suggest that we proceed with the amendments and leave the bill in committee; we can have our discussion here to-day and we can return to it if there are any further points which have not been made clear.

The difficulty I see is this. If this bill is sent to a special committee we will have the officers of the department who have had experience in administration, and

Food and Drugs Act
the}' can tell us precisely why they are asking for certain things. Let me illustrate; and I may say that I take my position with very little precise knowledge of the needs we have to meet, but I see an illustration of the danger facing us. In subsection (d) it is provided that the premises, equipment and technical qualifications of the staff of manufacturers preparing drugs mentioned or described in schedule B shall be inspected, and further in subsection 4 of the same section it is provided that any drug mentioned or described in schedule B shall be deemed to be adulterated if it has not been manufactured, tested and labelled in accordance with regulations made by the governor in council under this section. That is going pretty far. Let us take for example the question of the label. Some of these terms are copyrighted, I have no doubt, and it is quite conceivable that the department may fix as a standard one of these drugs which has been patented or given some sort of protection; they may say that that shall be the standard. If some other firm manufactures an equally good article not in the slightest degree adulterated, but labelled differently from the standardized article, the oroduct of the second firm would be deemed yo be adulterated under this act. That is an extreme case, of course, but that is what we ire facing, and I must say that under these drcumstances I rather look askance at this act. I am going to suggest again to the minister that the most reasonable thing to do is to send this bill to a special committee before which the officers of the department may appear. Let me again make it clear that I am not criticising the effort of the government to establish a first class workable act. I have always been in favour of such an act and stand behind the general principle of it but I must confess that some parts of this act give me some alarm.

I have just another question, and I might say in passing that I do not think I misunderstand the purposes of this amendment. I would like to refer for a moment to the inspection of premises, equipment and so on. Supposing you are dealing with drugs manufactured in England, manufactured by a firm which I like very much, Burroughs, Welcome and Company; how will your department inspect their premises and set a standard for their products? If that is not done the drugs manufactured by that company will be labelled as adulterated, and it leaves the door open to drastic action. I am sure that medical practitioners have some knowledge of standards, and I agree with the statement of the minister that these standards vary,
and in some cases are very low. But in Canada we practically accept the British Pharmacopoeia and the standards laid down by the ministry of health in England. Now the minister is going to introduce a system in Canada which will make it hard for us to accept an article manufactured in Great Britain.
Unless it comes up to the standard.

In the meantime
perhaps that drug will have been scattered all over Canada, and it will be quite a hardship to some of our practitioners who, notwithstanding that standard, would prefer to carry on with the same company.

I think my hon.
friend is entirely mistaken. If he will look at the schedule he will see that the list is very limited and that the drugs contained therein are very important. If the profession can secure a uniform standard of digitalis, for example, they will be glad to accept it. We are not entering a new field; it is known that the Council of Health of the League of Nations have already proceeded along this line, and are suggesting to the various countries that they standardize these preparations. The United States have gone even further, and have already set standards. This matter is one affecting trade and commerce and the protection of the public, and if it is the opinion of hon. members that this should go to a special committee I have no objection whatever because that would give an opportunity for further discussion which cannot take place in this House.
How does the minister propose to inspect the premises, equipment and so on of firms not in this country?

They will manufacture to our standards if they propose to sell in Canada. My friend speaks of Burroughs, Welcome and Company; that company are prepared to standardize, and wish to do so, and I think that is true of all the better manufacturers.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Northwest Territories Act, chapter 62 of the revised statutes, 1906, to provide that the commissioner in council may make ordinances for the levying of an export tax upon furs exported from the territories to any part of Canada, or to any foreign country.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: EXPORT TAX ON FURS
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen will remember that three years ago I introduced a similar resolution with a view to bringing down a bill to tax furs exported from the Northwest Territories. At that time, if my recollection serves me aright, all the provinces were not exacting a tax on furs. There was, however, a tax in force in the Yukon territory on furs for export, and principles embodied in the Yukon Fur Export Tax Ordinance will be included in the ordinance to be founded on this resolution. The provinces are anxious that we shall impose such a tax because furs are going out of the provinces very frequently, particularly from the northern districts of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and when the tax, or royalty as it is in Saskatchewan, is sought to be collected the provincial officers are told that the furs come from the Northwest Territories. We do not propose to tax fur used in the territories but only when it is exported therefrom, and the tax will be at the rate of so much per skin.
I will give full particulars on the second reading of the bill. Its main provision, however, is embodied in the resolution.

subtopic: EXPORT TAX ON FURS
speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to tell us when the provinces asked for the imposition of this export tax?

subtopic: EXPORT TAX ON FURS

I have a
letter signed- by the Hon. Mr. Hoadley of Alberta asking us to take some steps to protect that province inasmuch as when they seek to collect the provincial tax they are frequently told that the furs come from the Mackenzie district in the Northwest Territories and are therefore not taxable in Alberta. subtopic: EXPORT TAX ON FURS
speechtext:

subtopic: EXPORT TAX ON FURS
speechtext: In the provinces all fur is taxed; there are no exemptions. But we propose to exempt the fur used by the natives as well as any fur used by whites in the Northwest Territories. Only when the fur is leaving the territories will the tax be imposed. In that way we shall not be creating any hardship for the whites or natives who make their homes in that region. This is to be an export tax, and the same provision exists in the Yukon territory.

how does the minister propose to ascertain where the fur comes from? Furs, for instance, are frequently brought into Edmonton by trappers from very long distances. How does the minister propose to follow the fur that is produced in the Northwest Territories beyond the boundaries of any province?

anticipated that difficulty and are arranging to collect the tax inside the territories. speechtext:
After the many statements and arguments which have been advanced1 in this House during the course of this debate, anyone who attempts now to talk about the subject must in doing so lay himself open to the charge of obstructing the business of this House. It is not with that intention that I am taking part in this debate. If I must stand accused of obstructing the work of this House, I am perfectly satisfied to do so. I say that because it is a fact that the matter under discussion is of such great importance that I feel every opportunity should be taken to place the facts before the people of the country, in order that they may be stirred up, so that the ultimate result will be that this bill shall not pass.
It has been suggested1 from the other side of the House that the bill should be allowed to go to the committee at once. I do not favour that suggestion. The Georgian Bay Canal
Georgian bay canal promoters have been given ample time to do something to take advantage of the enormously valuable franchise granted first so long ago as 1894. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the House on this question. I must confess that since the debate started my understanding of the matter has become a little more clouded than it was before. I understood when the question was first brought up that it was opposed more as a matter of principle than for any other reason, but just on what principle it was opposed I am not quite so clear as I was when the hon. gentleman who opened the debate in opposition finished his remarks. I understood from his remarks that he was opposed to it largely because there had been a considerable delay in starting work under the charter which had been already granted. Since then hon. gentlemen who have spoken have discussed the matter from practically every angle and a large part of the argument both pro and con is, so far as I know, personal opinion or facts gained here and there in a haphazard manner. Any information upon which I can base my attitude has been gained in what is not a satisfactory method to myself, namely, by listening to the various arguments advanced, and by hearing the gossip and rumour in the

Georgian Bay Canal Company
corridors, lobbies and different parts of this building. If I had to vote on this bill tonight, as to whether we should grant this charter or not, with the information I have as to the charter I would vote against it. On the other hand if I were to be put in the position where I had to close my mind and say, No, we will take no chance on this, we will not give even an opportunity of ascertaining the facts by having them brought out before a committee, I would vote against such a motion, because I think I should be just as much to blame for refusing to allow myself to get those facts in a proper manner before a committee of the House as if I voted against the 'bill offhand.
I am not satisfied with the bill in its present state. I should like to see it somewhat amended; but the more I have heard and the more I have looked into it, the measure does not seem nearly as bad to me as it did originally. I must confess, Mr. Speaker and gentlemen, that my facts were collected, as I have suggested, from the discussion here and from hearsay. If I am wrong in any statement I may make I hope I shall be corrected, but I can only base my remarks upon the information which I have and give my vote in accordance therewith when the time comes to do so. I am told that this charter was granted originally in 1894, and the statute bears this out. I am told that the project has been enlarged from time to time, that in 1907 plans were made for a canal of nine feet, that the matter was taken up by this House, and that during the period from some time around 1908 till 1912 this government investigated the question of the Georgian bay canal and its feasibility, and a very lengthy report was prepared on the subject. That report is in the library, but I am not of a sufficient engineering turn of mind to avail myself of it; I do not think I would understand it even if I did try to peruse it. But the report is there, and I have not heard it stated that the route is not feasible. So matters were delayed apparently until 1912, and then it was decided that the project should take the form of a canal of twenty feet. The war broke out, and I do not think that any hon. membeT here will say that any company was remiss in its duty for not carrying out a large contract during a war period. Considerable time has elapsed since the war and yet nothing has been done. That I understand is true, but I also understand that plans were completed by the present holders of the charter for a canal of twenty-four feet, and 1924 was the date on which the company first filed the plans that are now before the government. Those plans were not accepted, but I find 
they were filed in sections up to1 1926, which is not very long ago. I understand that the first plan filed in 1924 was for that portion of the river from Montreal north-the proper place to start a canal, at the outlet-but for some reason best known to the government approval of the plans was withheld until all should be received. Now I notice that under section 18 of the original act this company cannot take any steps or do any construction work on the canal until the plans that have been filed are approved by the government. If there has been negligence and delay it would therefore appear that it was not on the part of the applicants, but on account of their plans not having been approved they have not been in a legal position to turn a sod or start construction work. I want to point out that those hon. gentlemen who have dealt upon heinousness of the offence that would be committed in giving a further extension to this charter, and those hon. gentlemen who believe strongly in public ownership, put through yesterday four distinct bills which involved the extension of railway charters. The first charter was granted in 1900 but was renewed from time to time up to the present. The next two charters have not been for an unusually long period before the public, but the fourth one was originally given in 1893, one year before the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company. I am not justifying the extension of these charters, I am merely bringing the facts to the attention of the House.

speechtext:
I am dealing now
with the objection, which has been strongly urged, that the time which has been allowed to elapse since the charter was originally granted is a reason why the extension sought here should not be allowed. I am not saying that the charters to which I have just referred should not have been enlarged, but what I do say is that there was not half an hour's discussion in this House-so far as I know, and I think I was present all the time-in opposition to the extension of these charters on the ground that they have been renewed too often. Yet they are all by private corporations. That looks rather peculiar to me in view of the great interest that is being taken in the present charter and the agitation to allow it to expire.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
I have dealt with the opposition to this charter on the ground of the delay that has taken place. Now there are one or two other reasons given by several members, the soundness of which I do not quite appreciate. For example they say that we have government canals which are operating without tolls, therefore why should we allow the canal to be built by private individuals on which tolls would be collected. I submit that argument would be much more logical if the conditions were reversed and you were putting a free canal in competition with a government canal charging tolls. But if the government canals are free and the private canal is charging tolls, what possible chance is there of the private canal doing business? How can they collect tolls unless the public are willing to pay them in order to avoid going the long way round and getting free transportation which would be more costly in the long run? I do not understand the logic of the argument which has been advanced, in that connection by at least three or four members of the House.
There is also the question of the claim to the power. I aim not going into the question of the legal ownership of the power, but I maintain that in so far as the navigable waters are concerned, and in so far as any waters are concerned which are apt to be now or hereafter of value to the Dominion as waterways, it is most objectionable to give any rights to private individuals which will close those waterways for navigation purposes in time to come, or in fact to give them under under any circumstances 'without, protecting the public interest. Ontario says, in the language of its representatives in this House, that it is entitled to the water-power. It may be so. If it is so, the owners of this charter have nothing when they get it renewed so far as power is concerned. That question can be disposed of by the courts that are appointed for that purpose.
I would point out this, however. Although I do not live in Ontario I try to keep in touch with the doings of the various provinces, and I understand that Ontario has leased its water-powers in the north country to private corporations at every place in which water-power is now being developed up there. I understand further that the people in that district are getting after the Ontario government to have the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission protect them against overcharges, but that they are not being given any assistance in that direction by the provincial government. The province of Ontario at the same time, I understand, is purchasing power from a private corporation called the Gatineau Power Company. I understand that the province of Ontario were
willing to give a lease of the Carillon falls to a private corporation for a consideration-a share of the rental. Now, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that all these arguments we have heard in favour of Ontario developing its own power do not look very good to the outsider in face of the fact that they are giving away their power in the northern section of the province and are buying power themselves from private corporations instead of developing their own power.

The Assistant Clerk read the article, as follows:
As was to be expected, the meeting of the special committee of council with the officials of the Abitibi Electric Development Company was devoid of any result as far as the lowering of the rate charged by the company is concerned, not because of any neglect on the part of the committee but rather on account of the peculiar independence which the Abitibi people are able to assume under existing circumstances and will be able to maintain until such time as the government sees fit to interfere and decide to protect not only our own municipality, but all others now here and yet to come, who are at the mercy of powerful corporations as far as power supply is concerned, when such is developed from the abundance of our natural water-powers, more especially here in the north where water-powers belong to the most valuable of natural resources.
It seems inconceivable that the government should have given away these natural resources belonging in the last end to the people, to private corporations for the purpose of exploiting these very people to whom such powers should belong, and who live in the very shadow of their magnificence. As a matter of fact we feel sure that the government has no intention of permitting such big stick methods.
Premier Ferguson gave an intimation to a recent delegation from the northern Ontario associated boards of trade that in the leasing of lands and water-powers, the people's interest had been fully safeguarded and that the big corporations must watch their steps and live up to conditions exacted at the time of such leases being granted and that he would see that they do it.
While we therefore fully agree with the committee's finding that nothing further can be gained by way of conferences with the Abitibi Electric Development Company, we do not at all agree with the conclusion arrived at that the only way out is the acceptance of the contract on the company's terms for a period of five years, without first having the case submitted to the government in a proper manner.
We have always maintained and still maintain that the abortive attempt to seek the government's intervention last summer was a farce pure and simple, and the people through their decision to vote down the by-law emphatically showed that they hold to this idea.
There is no intention whatever to show hostility against the power people in our continuing to advocate the introduction of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission into the dispute over the rates. The Abitibi people are well able to look after their interest in any presentation of their side to expert opinion, and on the other hand the Hydro-Electric Commission has no selfish interest in this case as they definitely refused some years ago to undertake the development of the water-powers in this district.

The old stock argument of comparing the rates which we are asked to consider as fair and reasonable with those paid by other municipalities along the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway is as fallacious as it is inapplicable.
In the first place, all the other towns in this district are at present moving heaven and earth to have the present rates reduced and are practically at the end of their patience and are preparing to take steps to press for government intervention.
Secondly, the position of Cochrane is far stronger to call for government intervention than any of the other municipalities along the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario. As far back as 1910 the government, through the then Minister of Lands and Forests, gave us the solemn assurance that the town of Cochrane would be fully protected if ever any of the surrounding water-powers would be leased to private corporations in the event of the HydroElectric Commission not taking up the development here. This was at a time when Iroquois falls was not even thought of, the advertising for tenders for that pulp concession appearing subsequent to the promise of the government to see the town fully protected with regard to future development around here.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to say one word further. This is a little place down in Prince Edward Island with a population of between five and six hundred and yields a gross postal revenue of about $3,000, out of which all the expenses of the post office have to be paid. In my judgment this is an unjustifiable expenditure of public money. In the budget debate recently I pointed out that if the Minister of Finance would sit down with a blue pencil he could save this country millions and millions of dollars by crossing out items of this kind almost on every page of the estimates. I have nothing against the village of Kensington, but I protest against the expenditure of public money in this way. It is not called for, it is not essential. We have thousands of objects in this country upon which the $12,000 could be profitably spent at the present time. My object in moving this motion is to protest against the government's course, and I ask the committee to support my action.

I would suggest to the Minis. ter of Public Works that as this item has crept into the main estimates 'by mistake, and there are several others of a similar character which have not been so fortunate, if he wishes to be consistent he should withdraw it until the others are revoted.

No, Mr. Chairman, I positively object to that. We took this matter up with the department in the proper way, and if my friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) has been negligent in regard to certain items in which his constituency is interested being included in the main estimates, that is no reason for withdrawing this particular vote. I want to tell the committee right here and now that this vote is going through. The site has been acquired, the eng'neer in charge has looked over itfae ground, plans have been prepared, and the work is proceeding. I am confident that hon. gentlemen qpposite will not think of supporting my hon. friend's motion.
Is the member correct in stating that this work is being proceeded with before the money is voted?

My information is that no work has been commenced and no expenditure made. There has been some preliminary investigation of the site, that is all. I might state to my hon. friend (Mr. Ernst) who is so greatly concerned about Mahone bay, and very properly so, that this is one of the items that appeared in the supplementary estimates of last year. It was submitted to the House by the government of which I was a member,
fThe Chairman.]
and it was also submitted by the government that succeeded us, of which some of my hon. friends opposite were members. It seems to me that when the time comes we might very well consider whether or not the supplementary estimates to which both parties were committed should not be adhered to. However, that is a matter for subsequent consideration. The item of Mahone bay, I may inform my hon. friend, is now voted.
How it is that some of the supplementary estimates have been included in the main estimates while others have been left out?

In making out the main estimates the intention first was that as a great deal of the supplementary votos could not be expended before the 31st of March, when they would expire, it might be as well to put into the main estimates everything of an urgent character that had hitherto been included in the supplementaries. That course was adhered to for the first half year I think. Then it was decided otherwise and instructions were given to discontinue this course. I do not want to lay any blame on any one because the instructions were given when I was present, but. apparently those instructions were not fully observed. Only a few items have crept in.

The minister's explanation
does not altogether satisfy me because I find that a number of the supplementary estimates are now in the main estimates, while other supplementary items have been left out.
That is just the situation.

Urgency does not appear to have been the sole consideration for including some of these supplementaries in the main estimates. One item that I refer to is in connection with a town where much more revenue is derived from the post office and the customs house than from some of the other places which have been fortunate enough to have their votes ieft in the main estimates. I agree with the hon. leader of the opposition that every Canadian is looking to the government to cut down expenditure.
Hear, hear.

If the government will
adhere to a definite policy of cutting down expenditure, I am quite willing to withdraw any applications that I am making for expenditures in my constituency.
But if it is going to be a matter of expenditures here and there for certain individuals who may belong to a particular party,

Supply-Public Works

Nova Scotia
then it is a case of everyone getting into the scramble as much as they possibly can. During the first four years I was down here I did -not make any effort to secure a post office for my constituents for the simple reason that we were all criticising the different governments for the huge expenditures contracted during the war and saying that we should get away from that sort of thing. But last year there seemed to be a disposition to loiosen up a little, and I made representations to the government for a post office in the town of Camrose. My request was met and an amount of $15,000 was placed in the supplementary estimates. We all know what happened during what has often been referred to as the hectic days of last session. Those supplementary estimates were not passed; but they were presented to the House at the beginning of this session and they were then all passed. I took it for granted that when the item of $15,000 for a post office at Camrose was included in that first vote the government would have treated it as fairly as the other items in those supplementary estimates. But much to my surprise, when the main estimates were brought down, although there were only two items in the supplementary estimates for Alberta, one is left and mine is cut out. This item of $12,000 of the bon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) is for a post office in a small village with only 500 of a population and only $3,000 of a revenue from that post office. The town of Camrose has a post office with a revenue of more than $16,500, and a subcustoms office with a revenue of more than $50,000 annually. We are renting two buildings in that town. The government owns a lot there and yet the vote for that post office has been thrown out, although we are going to expend money on a post office from which the revenue is less than one-fifth of that from the post office in the town of Camrose. I hope this has been an oversight, and the minister can assure me that when the supplementary estimates are brought down this year, this item will be included in time to take care of the post office at Camrose. The minister knows the town, and I think the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) will bear me out when I say that there is not a finer or more flourishing town in the whole province of Alberta and not a town which the citizens take a greater interest in developing and beautifying. It is a town with railways radiating out in eight different directions and with a large number of rural routes emanating from it. Outside of Calgary and Edmonton, it has the fourth largest revenue of the towns in Alberta. I feel sure that when this item was included
in the estimates last year the government must have given it careful consideration, and I hate to think they cut it out for any ulterior motive. I hope the minister can assure me that when the supplementary estimates are brought down he will comply with my request.

It is very interesting to
hear about other post offices, but this is a concrete case which brings up the policy of the government in regard to these matters. We have the facts; there is no dispute. This is a little hamlet with a population of five or six hundred where there is a gross post office revenue of about $3,000 or, I suppose, about one-half that amount net. Is it the policy of the government to expend $12,000 of the taxes of the people of this country in establishing for political purposes a post office iu that riding? That is the question before the committee at this moment. The hon. member for Prince says in the most emphatic manner that this committee will pass this item and now he nods his head. What arrangement he has with the government I know not, but it looks as though he had a fast and binding arrangement of some kind.
Let me ask the Minister of Public Works how he can justify this expenditure. Is this the policy he is going to pursue throughout Canada? Does he think it right to collect and expend the taxpayers' money in this way at a time when, if we believe the Minister of Finance-and we must believe him-every dollar we can collect is necessary to meet out obligations this year, and in fact we shall have to go out and borrow money to do so. .Nevertheless without a pretence of excuse as regards public expenditure and the convenience of the people, the minister says; I want the -committee to vote $12,000 to erect a public building in the constituency of Prince, not in a village, but in a hamlet. I protest that that is a wrongful expenditure, I do not care in whose riding it is. Ontario is full of hamlets larger than Kensington, and with greater revenues; so is the west, and I protest against spending the public money in these -places. If we had -a treasury that was full and overflowing; if we had no Obligations maturing, different considerations might arise. But at the present moment it is improper to spend this money under these conditions. I protest as vigorously as I can, and I desire to have the sense of the committee taken on this question.

I am rather
surprised at the insinuations that have been thrown out by my hon. friend as regards the town of Kensington, which happens to be in

Supply-Public Works-Nova Scotia
the county which I have the honour to represent. I wish to say emphatically that this is not given as a bribe to the people of that good county or to the town of Kensington, for their votes, because the people there are too intelligent to be bribed and they will vote as they please, irrespective of post offices or anything else.
Then the hon. member does not need this.

The hon. member is right. There is no need of it for that purpose. The hon. member for Camrose stated that the government at the present time is renting a public building or two public buildings there for post office purposes. In the town of Kensington we had a disastrous fire which wiped out pretty nearly all the business portion including the Bank of Nova Scotia and I think the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the town was practically depleted of buildings. This post office is in the outskirts of the town in a house where it has been for the last forty years. The town has been rebuilt very rapidly ; it is growing fast. It is in the best agricultural section of the province and a large number of farmers are retiring and moving into it. As I pointed out, a large surrounding country is served by six or seven rural routes from that post office. At the present time the accommodations are not satisfactory; they are not what the town deserves; they are not what the surrounding country deserves, and this is being asked for only as a matter of justice to the town. I emphatically resent the reflections that have been cast upon the town of Kensington when it is said that this is done for political purposes. I again appeal to the committee to support the item and, in doing so, members will be doing justice not only to the town of Kensington, but to the surrounding country which is obliged to use that post office, and to the rural districts that are served from it. This vote was passed at a former session. It was in the supplementary estimates which were passed last year. The work was not proceeded with, and the item was passed again at the beginning of this session. I asked to have the item again inserted in the main estimates, because I knew that the building could not be completed before the 31st of March, when the-other vote would lapse. I cannot see any reason in the world now why the House should attempt to cut out this item after it has gone so far. My hon. friends should have taken objection to this amount last year or in

the early part of this session; I submit it is now too late in the day to cut down this item.

I would suggest to the minister that since no site has yet been purchased in Kensington, there are a number of sites available in towns in my constituency upon which buildings might be erected. In the town of Bridgetown in my constituency a site was purchased for a post office, just before the election of 1925, but apparently the electors did not vote right and nothing has been done. I would suggest that this $12,000 be used on the site already owned in that town.

I recall that when the supplementary estimates were before the House there was some discussion on this same item, and I recall that the member for that constituency then admitted that $12,000 was too much money. He was honest with the House and he made that admission, which I find recorded in Hansard as follows.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry, but it is not permissible to read from or refer to a debate which took place during this session.

Very well; I will not quote the words but will just refer to them generally. The hon. member made it quite plain that $12,000 was too much money for the requirements of Kensington. The sum of $12,000 did look to me like a rather large expenditure for a village of some 500 people, and the member for that constituency admitted that they were not seriously going to ask for that amount, but that they wanted enough to erect a suitable building there. That was the sum and substance of his remarks. Possibly the amendment of the leader of the opposition would not leave quite enough to put up a building which would suit the people, because the amount remaining would be only one dollar, but I would appeal to the minister to reduce this item by one-half at least, and possibly a little more. If it were reduced in that way it would leave plenty of money to erect a building suitable to the needs of that village of five hundred. The hon. member said there was a good country around that village, but you can drop into every town and village of this Dominion and find a fairly good country around it. I have a number of villages and towns in my own constituency around which there is magnificent country; there is one town with a population of 1,000 with the post office in an old shack of a building. I guess the people do not vote right; I am afraid after all that this is

Supply-Public Works-Nova Scotia
the real reason for this $12,000 expenditure, and I agree with the leader of the opposition that it is time to call a halt to this sort of political expenditure. We talk here about reducing our expenditures and taking care of our national debt and curtailing unnecessary outlays, yet we drift along regardless. This is just one small example of how thousands of dollars are squandered unnecessarily. I will certainly support the amendment, but I would like to see a compromise agreed upon reducing the estimate by about one-half. By so doing we would thoroughly satisfy the hon. member for that constituency in view of what he really asked the House to do earlier this session.

It is not my desire to throw any cold water on an estimate for post offices or public works in the maritime provinces, because I believe the Dominion of Canada owes to the maritimes millions of dollars. But speaking of post offices I wish to say that in my constituency there is a post office which turns into the treasury of Canada a net revenue of $377,000 per annum. I refer to the city of Moncton, which has a population of about 20,000 or 21,000. In spite of the fact that that post office turns in a larger net revenue than any other city or constituency of the same size in Canada, we have not been able to get a new building. We have been endeavouring for some time to secure a new post office there, and the government have purchased a very fine property assessed by the city iat $32,200. This property was purchased by the government for $49,000, [DOT] but the tenant who previously owned the property was permitted to occupy the premises for $40 per month up until January 1. I think any city or constituency whose poet office turns in such a large net revenue is entitled to consideration in so far as public buildings and post offices are concerned. I would like to see something done in that city, where the net return is more than double the expenditure on public works this year for the whole province of New Brunswick. I would draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General to these facts and ask them to consider seriously doing justice to the constituency which I represent.

I am not opposed to the expenditure of money on public buildings, on principle; I think there has been altogether too little money spent in that way in recent years, and only the exigencies of post-war financing can excuse the Dominion government for its neglect of the public buildings in our small towns. The other day I was
reading an account by an immigrant of his journey to his home in Alberta, in which he described the towns through which he passed as conglomerations of small wooden 'huts. I think there is something wrong when, after all these years of our prosperity, our prairie towns are deficient in substantial buildings. In my own town of Swan River we have a population of about 900 and our post office does a business amounting to probably $4,000 or $5,000 yearly. Yet for all these years the Dominion government has been carrying on its. business in a building on one of our main thoroughfares Which can only be described as a Shack. Around that building we have other structures Which are quite substantial; we have two bank buildings which are a credit to the town, and our provincial government has built for. its telephone service, right next to the Dominion government post office, a building which puts the Dominion building quite in the shade.
I am not finding fault with the government for not proceeding with the construction of a new building. I realize the circumstances that have been prevalent for a number of years, but I want to say it is rather hard on those of us who are not attached to the predominant party. In the last election my opponent managed to take quite a.few votes from me because he was able to promise a new post office. The then Postmaster General during the election visited my home town. I do not know what he said to my opponent but after he had left my opponent immediately gave it out that a new post * office was to foe fouilt in the town. Not being in the confidence of a predominant party I was not in a similar position to make a promise. I mention this because I think there is a good deal of insincerity in the amendment that has been moved. I mean that this is not a thing that is characteristic merely of the party in power. It was also characteristic of the party that wished to be in power. However, if I thought the Minister of Public Works had any consistent policy in regard to public buildings I should be most willing to give him my support. I think that such a policy might be possible -not a policy to favour constituencies that have been politically favourable, but a policy that would do justice to the status of the Dominion government in hundreds of our small towns throughout Canada. After all it might be a very good business proposition for the government to erect a public building in some of our small towns. For instance, the department in my town pays no less than about $800 a year for the use of three small rooms in which to transact their forestry

Supply-Public Works

Nova Scotia
business. It seems to me that a modest building, not a very big one, which would house not only the Forestry branch but also the post office branch, would be a business investment. I do not think that if it was wisely planned it could possibly be a loss to the Dominion government. But that is only one side of the situation. The side that appeals to me most is this:	that when we have
public buildings of a substantial character or of a more or less architectural success it lends an air of stability to any community in which they are placed, and that is one thing we lack sadly in the west. Surely the Dominion government, as times go on and its finances begin to look up, will enter earnestly into a policy of providing in our small communities some symbol -of its own existence which people may look to and respect, and after all that is a good deal. Our Dominion government is a remote thing to most of our communities and some suitable public building in which its own business is transacted would I am sure-especially in a good many western communities where the Dominion government is a far-away, vague and remote thing-have the effect of begetting in the minds of the people, the young people, of those communities a new sense of respect and attachment to the central authority. I do not think we always ought to consider the material aspect and the political aspect of questions; we should consider the patriotic, the national aspect also. I have noticed that it is possible for a few thousand dollars nowadays to construct public buildings which when completed have a certain architectural appeal. Only recently in our town a certain dairy company built a dairy. Now you.would think that a modern dairy company in placing a building in a town in which to carry on its business would not have any idea but that of utility. This company, however, came into our small town and built a structure which from the architectural point of view is all that could be desired. And yet our Dominion government is carrying on its business in the same town in a building which cannot be characterized as anything but a shack. I cannot find it in my heart to support the amendment, because of my experience in the election when the then Postmaster General came into my community and apparently gave my opponent to understand that if he were returned the community would get a fine postal building. That makes me disposed not to accept this amendment seriously. Moreover I do not know the needs of the community for which my hon. friend speaks. But if they compare at all with some of the western communities

where the public building is so very poor, I have a great deal of sympathy for them. As to the building in this case I hope it is not political like the one that was to go up in my own town.
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. If I understood him aright he said that I had promised a public building in his town if his opponent was elected.

I never said the hon. gentleman promised a public building. I have more regard for the hon. gentleman's common sense than to think he would come into a community during election time and promisp offhand a public building, but I do say that after my hon. friend's visit my opponent did give it out that if he were returned, there would be a public building erected in my town. There were quite a number of other matters I have not thought worth while to bring up on the floor of the House because it has not been my custom to air election matters in that way. I only mentioned this because I thought it was an opportune occasion to do so.

I should just like to say that I am not responsible for statements the hon. gentleman's opponent may have made. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that I had promised a public building if his opponent was elected. I wish to state that I promised no public building in any place in this Dominion. Furthermore, although I was * not going to take any part in this debate at all but simply vote with the leader of the opposition, I wish to say that I am entirely in accord with the leader of the opposition in this matter and I will tell you why: not only have all these sites been long in existence that have been mentioned here to-night, but there are sites all over this Dominion of Canada that were bought long ago for the purpose of putting up public buildings. For example, right in the constituency of the Minister of Labour, in the town of Fort Frances-which has a population not of five hundred people as in the case of this little village; but of 3,600 to 4,500; I do not know the exact figure-a site was bought before the war, and it is there still with not a public building in the whole town put up by any Dominion government. They were using a little ramshackle building until recently, when they rented other public offices. Fort Frances is one of the most prosperous little towns in all Ontario, a very fine little industrial centre. It has been trying since 1911 to get justice in the matter of a public building, but it

Supply-Public Works-Nova Scotia
receives no consideration, at all, While a little village in Prince Edward Island gets $12,000 for a public building, which is more than was asked for. I took the attitude in the town of Fort Frances in the last election-I had the courage to do that-that no public buildings should be constructed until our taxation had been lessened and financial conditions improved, but that when a start was made, Fort Frances should get as early consideration as any other town. I believe that is the right policy to-day, and certainly if buildings are to be constructed Fort Frances should receive earlier consideration than this little village of five hundred people. In addition, Fort Frances already has the site. I have visited my good friend the deputy minister on different occasions in regard to Fort Frances and a number of other places that deserve a public building, and he informs me that there are some eighty or ninety places in the Dominion Where sites have been bought for public buildings away back in the past, around 1910 or 1911, but where no buildings have been put up-I may not have given the exact number, but the minister will correct me if I am wrong. Under these circumstances, a vote such as this certainly should not pass the House.

It appears to me that
the question before us to-night is not whether there should be a post office building at Kensington, but rather a question of policy as * to whether post office buildings should be constructed at all at this time, and if they are built, where are they the most urgently required. In other words, should these plums be handed around as political favours? The vote to-night will apparently decide whether or not the government is to go ion with a program of simply placing these buildings wherever they choose for political purposes, or whether they intend to use the various votes that may pass the House for the benefit of the country at large.
I have no particular axe to grind. If I had, I could give instances probably much stronger than any that have been given to-night. I might mention my own town, for instance, where the post office revenue has averaged over $20,000 a year and where the customs revenue has averaged about $500,000 annually for many years, where there is also an Indian department under my genial friend the Minister of the Interior, and all of them occupying rented buildings. no such case arises as this building that is proposed to be constructed at Kensington in Prince Edward Island. I asked the Minister of Public Works whether it was the policy of the government to allow one member representing one particular constituency to control patronage in another constituency. The Minister of Public Works has not thought it advisable to give a direct answer, and I therefore address the question to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I imagine it
must have been the modesty of my colleague, not wishing to take too much credit to himself. The government controls the patrondge, and with respect to public works the govern-menit speaks through the Minister of Public Works.

Item agreed to.
Edmundston-public building, $2,000.
What is that for?
This is required to complete the building erected during 1925, 1926 and 1927.

We have had a lot of
buildings erected at Edmundston. Is this for the post office or customs?

Georgian Bay Canal Company
The post office.

The post office building
was erected three or four years ago.

What has been the total
cost of the Edmundston post office?

There has been so far
expended $71,255, and the amount required to complete it is $2,000, making a total of $73,255.
Item agreed to.

We have had a pretty
full day, and the government I think will agree that they have had no unfair opposition. It is now late, and I would suggest that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the
committee rises I would ask my hon. friend if he would have any objection to our calling one item in the Mines department, so that we can go into committee of supply on that department on Thursday, which otherwise we could not do except by unanimous consent.

I do not think there is
any objection to that.
Mines and Geological Survey-for organization and equipment of the Explosives divisions, under the Explosives Act, Chap. 31, 4-5 George V, $10,000.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is the
same as last year.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11 p.m.
Wednesday, March 9, 1927
